quote: that the usual way of visualizing the Prisoner’s Dilemma has a severe flaw
content: The "audacious assertion" is standard textbook doctrine. In game theory, payoffs are utilities by definition, not dollars or years in prison. Textbooks from Luce and Raiffa onward warn that if players care about each other the payoffs must be rewritten, and the game may no longer be a Prisoner's Dilemma (Luce & Raiffa, Games and Decisions, 1957; book, no DOI). Experimental economists design around this and distinguish material payoffs from utilities in their reports. The paperclip version is a vivid illustration, not a correction of the field.

quote: a neurologically intact human being cannot pretend to be genuinely, truly selfish
content: Many people don't need to pretend. In one-shot experimental dilemmas roughly half of subjects defect. Sally (1995)'s meta-analysis of more than a hundred experiments found average cooperation rates around 47%, falling with repetition. Burton-Chellew & West (2013) found that much of the remaining "cooperation" in public-goods games reflects confusion about the payoffs rather than prosocial preference, since it persisted when subjects knew they were playing against computers. Humans are more selfish, and more confused, than the essay supposes.

quote: And no, you can’t instruct people being initially introduced to game theory to pretend they’re completely selfish
content: The evidence suggests you can, in the sense that matters for behavior. Economics students, trained in exactly this framing, defect in Prisoner's Dilemma games significantly more often than students of other subjects (Frank, Gilovich & Regan 1993). Whether that reflects who chooses economics or what economics teaches is disputed. But the evidence doesn't show that the selfish framing can't be adopted.

quote: We’re born with a sense of fairness, honor, empathy, sympathy, and even altruism—the result of our ancestors’ adapting to play the iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma.
content: Both halves are doubtful. Fairness preferences are not present at birth in any strong sense. Egalitarian sharing develops between ages three and eight and increasingly favors the in-group (Fehr, Bernhard & Rockenbach 2008), and adult fairness norms vary widely across societies with market integration and social structure (Henrich et al. 2005). And two-player repeated reciprocity is only one candidate explanation. It is generally thought insufficient to explain cooperation in large groups of non-kin, and its competitors include indirect reciprocity, partner choice and cultural group selection.

quote: In fact, I don’t think rational agents should always defect in one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemmas, when the other player will cooperate if it expects you to do the same.
content: The promised route to rational cooperation doesn't work in the scenario the essay builds. Formal results on cooperation in one-shot dilemmas require each agent to have access to, and be able to verify, the other's decision procedure. That includes program equilibrium, where each player's strategy can depend on the other's source code (Tennenholtz 2004), and its later proof-based descendants. The True Prisoner's Dilemma stipulates the opposite: no history, no communication, no future interaction, an alien optimizer from another dimension. The cited manuscript was unpublished and couldn't close that gap. As stated, the P.S. is a promise with nothing behind it.
